name: Splat Sorting and Composition
text:
# Splat Sorting and Composition

Also called: Splat Composition

## Overview
Splat Sorting and Composition is the [object-order rendering](#22-object-order-rendering.md) step that transforms a set of transformed volumetric primitives into a final 2D image by resolving depth occlusion and blending transparency. It solves the order-dependent transparency problem inherent in [splatting](#23-splatting.md), where incorrect draw order leads to visual artifacts, by sorting primitives along the view direction and accumulating their contributions via [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md). It is distinguished from ray-casting methods by [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) along sheets (all pixels for a set of voxels simultaneously) rather than along rays, and from order-independent transparency (OIT) methods by relying on explicit depth sorting to enable hardware-accelerated rasterization [S1][S2, S3, unofficial][S7, unofficial][S10, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized [G].

1.  **[Primitive Representation](#11838-primitive-representation.md):** The volume is decomposed into primitives [G]. Each primitive $k$ is defined by its position $\mathbf{p}_k$, density/extinction coefficient $g_k$ or $\rho_k$, and a reconstruction kernel $h$ (typically a Gaussian) [S1][S6, unofficial][S10, unofficial].
2.  **Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., [shear-warp](#24-shear-warp.md)) [S2, S3, unofficial][S4]. For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., [EWA splatting](#1069-ewa-splatting.md)) to account for foreshortening [S6, unofficial][S10, unofficial].
3.  **Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane [G]. The contribution of a voxel $D$ to a screen point $(x,y)$ is determined by the [footprint function](#4731-footprint-function-mechanism.md) $F(x,y)$, which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction [S2, unofficial][S6, unofficial][S10, unofficial]:
    $$ F(x,y) = \int h(x-x_D, y-y_D, z) \, dz $$
    The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density:
    $$ P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) $$
4.  **Compositing:** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image [G]. This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1][S2, S3, unofficial][S7, unofficial]. Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) [S10, unofficial].
5.  **Hardware [Acceleration](#18-acceleration.md):** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1][S2, S3, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Stop-the-pop](1472-stop-the-pop.md)
[Stop-the-pop](#1472-stop-the-pop.md) (STP) is a hierarchical sorting and culling technique designed to mitigate temporal popping artifacts in volume splatting, specifically those caused by view-inconsistent sorting of Gaussians along the ray. While standard global per-tile sorting can lead to flickering when Gaussian depths shift across frames, STP groups primitives into coarse depth bins and performs sorting only within the bin covering depth discontinuities. This approach removes popping artifacts without sacrificing the rendering speed achieved by hardware-accelerated rasterization. Choose this method when rendering animated scenes with dynamic Gaussians where temporal stability is critical and full global sorting is too expensive.

### [Order Independent Transparency for Point-Based Models](2150-order-independent-transparency-for-point-based-models.md)
This method renders transparent point-based models on GPUs in an order-independent manner by extending depth-peeling techniques to deferred-shaded multi-pass splatting. It reconstructs transparent layers iteratively from closest to farthest, avoiding the need for explicit per-pixel fragment sorting. It distinguishes itself from siblings like [Stop-the-pop](1472-stop-the-pop.md) by using iterative layer reconstruction with deferred shading. Choose this method when the number of transparent layers is small and bounded (typically 3 or 4), allowing for high-quality transparency without sorting overhead, at the cost of multiple rendering passes.

### [Detached Hybrid Transparency](10048-detached-hybrid-transparency.md)
[Detached Hybrid Transparency](#10048-detached-hybrid-transparency.md) (DHT) is a technique used during the training of volumetric representations (specifically 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md)) to stabilize the optimization process when [Early Ray Termination (ERT)](#7920-opacity-based-early-termination.md) is enabled. While ERT improves rendering speed by skipping distant or transparent primitives, it introduces gradient bias because the skipped contributions are not backpropagated. DHT resolves this by approximating the color contribution of the skipped "tail" of Gaussians using unordered alpha blending and applying a stop-gradient operator to detach this approximation from the gradient computation. This allows the use of aggressive [early termination](#4675-early-termination.md) thresholds during training without causing the rapid Gaussian expansion and convergence failure seen in naive implementations. Choose this method specifically for the training phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting to enable fast ERT without destabilizing the optimizer.

### [Sorting Algorithms](14243-sorting-algorithms.md)
[Sorting Algorithms](#14243-sorting-algorithms.md) in volume rendering splatting reorder volumetric primitives (typically 3D Gaussian splats) by depth to ensure correct [front-to-back alpha blending](#1141-front-to-back-compositing-unpremultiplied.md). This solves the order-dependent transparency problem inherent in splatting, where incorrect draw order leads to visual artifacts. Unlike siblings that may use partial ordering or hardware-specific tricks, this family focuses on generating a strict depth-sorted index buffer for the rasterizer. Choose this method when a strict, globally consistent draw order is required for correct alpha blending in standard hardware pipelines.

### Splat-Every-Sample Composition
A composition method where every sample is splatted, compared against [slice-by-slice (sheet buffer) splatting](#2110-slice-by-slice-sheet-buffer-splatting.md) [S2, unofficial]. Splat-every-sample produces darker images due to incorrect visibility determination. It achieves better performance by avoiding per-slice additions [S2, unofficial].

### Order Independent EWA Volume Splatting
A novel order independent EWA volume splatting method that unifies the advantages of previous OI techniques and provides an efficient high-speed approximation by exploiting the analytical expression of elliptical Gaussian kernels used for the noise [S3, unofficial]. It computes a fast view-dependent approximation of accumulated densities along viewing directions using a per-pixel projective volume rendering approach and projects the spatially bound kernel functions directly (splat them) thanks to their analytic representation [S3, unofficial]. Unlike [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) which requires hundreds of evaluations per pixel and is computationally demanding for [procedural noise](#1799-procedural-noise-functions.md), this method provides interactive visualization [S3, unofficial]. Unlike EWA volume splatting which requires time-consuming back-to-front ordering and introduces rasterization overhead due to overlapping ellipses, this OI method gets rid of ordering to trade realism for speed [S3, unofficial].

### Object-level rendering
A method to segment splats by object and prioritize them based on their summed contribution, allowing high-quality representation for important objects and low-quality for others [S4]. It segments splats belonging to specific objects (manually or via 2D segmentation methods), finds the contribution of splats within this segmentation to determine the importance of objects, and prioritizes objects based on their contribution to the scene, sending higher-quality representations of important objects [S4].

### Composability without Constraints
A method to compose multiple 3D objects/scenes by concatenating rank components along the rank dimension and summing ranks, supporting arbitrary affine transformations and occlusion handling [S5]. It concatenates rank components along the rank dimension for each object $n$, calculates total ranks $R = \sum_{n=1}^{N} R_n$, and records transformation matrix $T_n \in \mathbb{R}^{4 \times 4}$ for each object [S5]. The density and color are computed as $\sigma_{i,n}, c_{i,n} = f_\Theta(T_n x_i, R_n d)$ where $T_n$ includes translation $t_n$, rotation $R_n$, and scale $s_n$, and $x_i$ is homogeneous coordinate, $d$ is unit viewing direction [S5]. Opacity is $\alpha_i = 1 - \exp(-\delta_i \sum_{n=1}^{N} \sigma_{i,n})$ and Color is $c_i = \sum_{n=1}^{N} \phi_N(\sigma_{i,n}) c_{i,n}$ where $\phi_N$ is the softmax function applied to densities [S5]. Occlusion between different objects must be handled correctly by summing densities from all objects to calculate opacity and weighting color by density after softmax [S5].

### Composite-Only Splatting
The most basic splatting method where object points are traversed in depth order, assigned color/opacity, splatted into screen buffers, and composited with the present image [S6, unofficial]. Color bleeding and slight sparkling artifacts in animated viewing may be noticeable because interpolation and compositing operations cannot be separated due to pre-integration of the basis kernel [S6, unofficial].

### Back-to-front Splat Sorting
A compositing technique for splats ([oriented ellipses](#7934-oriented-ellipse-splatting.md)) that sorts them back-to-front relative to a camera viewpoint to ensure correct translucent blending [S7, unofficial]. When `cameraPositionProvider` is null, the `SplatNode` automatically sorts its splats for the scene camera's current position. If `cameraPositionProvider` is provided, the node sorts splats for the viewpoint returned by that provider instead of the scene camera. The sorting is performed on a background thread whenever the camera moves [S7, unofficial]. Without a `cameraPositionProvider` (and thus without sorting), the compositing order remains as loaded, causing visual popping artifacts when orbiting the camera [S7, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of splatting as an [object-order volume rendering](#10725-object-order-volume-rendering.md) technique was introduced in the early 1990s, with foundational work by Westover (1990) and Levoy (1990) establishing the use of kernel functions to project volumetric data onto the image plane [S6, unofficial][S10, unofficial]. The specific application of sorting and alpha compositing for Gaussian primitives has become central to modern [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) techniques, popularized by Kerbl et al. (2023) [S1]. The Khronos Group's `KHR_gaussian_splatting` extension formalized the sorting and composition rules for interoperable rendering of Gaussian splats, specifying back-to-front sorting based on camera-to-mean distance and the [standard alpha blending](#5697-hardware-alpha-blending-compositing.md) equation [S1]. Recent developments have focused on optimizing this step through hierarchical sorting (Stop-the-pop) [S1][S4], order-independent transparency [S1], and training-time stability mechanisms (Detached Hybrid Transparency) [S1].
